paragraphs.title: The Destruction of Zion and the Temple

answers: The Lord’s anger and the destruction of Zion
A joyful feast in Jerusalem
The rebuilding of the city walls
easy.explanation: The verses describe the Lord’s anger and the destruction of Israel, Judah, Zion, and the sanctuary.
easy.q: What do the opening verses describe?

answers: They were enlarged
The Lord cast off the altar and abhorred his sanctuary
They were protected by the king
easy.explanation: Verse 7 says that the Lord cast off his altar and abhorred his sanctuary.
easy.q: What happened to the altar and sanctuary?

answers: They led the people from the Temple
They remained in the city
They were among the Gentiles
easy.explanation: Verse 9 says, “Her king and her princes are among the Gentiles.”
easy.q: Where were the king and princes?

answers: There was great mourning, and the city lost its protection
The city became stronger
The people received immediate comfort
medium.explanation: The walls, gates, and bars were destroyed, causing the city to mourn and languish.
medium.q: What resulted from the destruction of the city and its defenses?

answers: Songs of Judah
Fortified places belonging to Judah
The elders of Judah
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to Judah’s fortified places, which the Lord threw down.
medium.q: What are the “strong holds of the daughter of Judah”?

answers: Prophecy, feasting, and rebuilding the gates
Joy, comfort, and return
The destruction of the Temple and walls, the exile of leaders, and the loss of law and vision
medium.explanation: The passage moves from destruction to the exile of the king and princes and then to the absence of law and prophetic vision.
medium.q: Which sequence correctly describes the collapse of the kingdom?

answers: The destruction is described as though the Lord acted against Israel as an enemy
The enemies had no part in the destruction
The Lord left the land without doing anything
challenge.explanation: The comparison emphasizes the severity of the Lord’s judgment against the city.
challenge.q: What does the statement “The Lord was as an enemy” show about the destruction?

answers: There were many teachers and prophets
There was no longer an evident source of guidance and hope
The people quickly returned to the Temple
challenge.explanation: The verse says that the law was no more and that the prophets found no vision from the Lord.
challenge.q: What is the significance of there being no law or vision at the end of the passage?

answers: The children asked for food
Passersby hissed at the city
The kingdom, leaders, altar, sanctuary, walls, and gates were all affected
challenge.explanation: The passage mentions government, leaders, holy places, and defensive structures.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the destruction affected the city’s symbols as well as its buildings?

paragraphs.title: The Mourning of the People and the Hunger of Children

answers: They sit upon the ground and keep silence
They lead songs of victory
They rebuild the walls
easy.explanation: The elders sit on the ground, cast dust upon their heads, and wear sackcloth.
easy.q: How are the elders of the daughter of Zion described?

answers: They go out to battle
They hang down their heads and mourn
They distribute food
easy.explanation: The virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground.
easy.q: What do the virgins of Jerusalem do?

answers: Where is the king?
When will the Temple be rebuilt?
Where is corn and wine?
easy.explanation: The children ask, “Where is corn and wine?”
easy.q: What do the children ask their mothers?

answers: The children faint and grow weak from lack of food
The children go into the streets to celebrate
The children distribute food to passersby
medium.explanation: The children and sucklings swoon in the streets because of hunger.
medium.q: What is the connection between hunger and the children in the streets?

answers: The speaker is calm and joyful
The speaker is overwhelmed with grief
The speaker is preparing for battle
medium.explanation: The failing eyes and troubled bowels express intense sorrow over the destruction of the people.
medium.q: What does the expression “Mine eyes do fail with tears” communicate?

answers: The children pray, the elders fight, and the virgins celebrate
The elders and virgins mourn, while the children suffer from hunger
The virgins build, the children eat, and the elders sing
medium.explanation: The verses describe mourning elders and virgins and starving children.
medium.q: Which order correctly describes the groups in the passage?

answers: It shows that every part of the population was affected
It limits the destruction to one group
It describes only ordinary family life
challenge.explanation: The passage includes old people, young women, children, and infants, showing the widespread nature of the disaster.
challenge.q: Why does mentioning the elders, virgins, and children strengthen the description of the destruction?

answers: The children are asking for decorations
The lack of food has become a daily cry
The city is filled with feasts
challenge.explanation: The children’s question reveals their desperate hunger and the absence of food.
challenge.q: What can be understood from the question, “Where is corn and wine?”

answers: He raises the city gates
His eyes are filled with tears and his inward parts are troubled
He goes out to meet the enemy
challenge.explanation: The mourner describes his failing eyes, troubled bowels, and poured-out liver.
challenge.q: Which physical detail expresses the mourner’s grief?

paragraphs.title: No Comfort and the Failure of the Prophets

answers: As small and easy to heal
As great as the sea and apparently without healing
As a cause for great joy
easy.explanation: The speaker says, “Thy breach is great like the sea: who can heal thee?”
easy.q: How is the breach of Jerusalem described?

answers: They did not reveal the people’s iniquity or turn them from captivity
They failed to repair the walls
They refused to give food to the children
easy.explanation: The prophets saw vain and foolish things instead of discovering the people’s iniquity and turning them back.
easy.q: What was wrong with the prophets?

answers: They expressed only sorrow
They ignored it
They rejoiced, hissed, and showed hostility
easy.explanation: The enemies opened their mouths, hissed, gnashed their teeth, and rejoiced over Jerusalem’s fall.
easy.q: How did the enemies respond to the destruction?

answers: They awakened the people to repentance
They failed to reveal the iniquity and did not turn the people back
They prevented the enemies from rejoicing
medium.explanation: The prophets did not discover the iniquity or turn away the captivity of the people.
medium.q: What was the effect of the prophets’ false visions?

answers: Empty and unreliable messages
Excellent food
Strong defenses
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to messages without truth or value.
medium.q: In context, what does “vain and foolish things” mean?

answers: Both observe the ruined city and react to it
Both rebuild the city
Both ask the children for food
medium.explanation: Passersby clap and hiss at Jerusalem, while the enemies also hiss and mock her destruction.
medium.q: What do passersby and enemies have in common in the description?

answers: The disaster is so great that no comparison seems adequate
The speaker has found a more beautiful city
The speaker is offering a practical rebuilding plan
challenge.explanation: The repeated questions emphasize how difficult it is to find anything comparable to Jerusalem’s suffering.
challenge.q: What is the force of the repeated question, “What thing shall I liken to thee”?

answers: She was an unknown city
She was regarded as beautiful and joyful throughout the earth
She had already been abandoned before the destruction
challenge.explanation: The enemies refer to Jerusalem as “The perfection of beauty” and “The joy of the whole earth.”
challenge.q: What does the enemies’ description of Jerusalem suggest about her former condition?

answers: The enemies rejoice after the Lord has fulfilled what he had devised and spoken
The enemies canceled the Lord’s word
The judgment never came to pass
challenge.explanation: Verse 17 says that the Lord fulfilled his word and then caused the enemy to rejoice.
challenge.q: How are the enemies’ words connected with the Lord’s judgment?

paragraphs.title: Cry, Prayer, and the Depth of Suffering

answers: To the enemy
To the children’s mothers
To the Lord
easy.explanation: The passage says, “Their heart cried unto the Lord.”
easy.q: To whom is the city’s cry directed?

answers: In the night, at the beginning of the watches
Only at noon
At the end of a feast
easy.explanation: She is told to arise and cry out in the night, at the beginning of the watches.
easy.q: When is the daughter of Zion told to arise and cry?

answers: For the enemies
For the young children fainting from hunger
For Judah’s fortresses
easy.explanation: The prayer asks the Lord to consider the young children who faint from hunger.
easy.q: For whom is the prayer especially made?

answers: Remain silent and hide
Pour out her heart and lift up her hands before the Lord
Leave the city and build a wall
medium.explanation: She is told to pour out her heart like water and lift up her hands toward the Lord.
medium.q: What is the daughter of Zion told to do in prayer?

answers: The famine, the slain priest and prophet, and the suffering people
The rebuilding of the Temple
Only the enemies’ celebration
medium.explanation: The prayer asks the Lord to see the extreme hunger and the deaths of the priest, prophet, young, and old.
medium.q: What does the speaker ask the Lord to behold and consider?

answers: Do not stop crying and praying
Celebrate without interruption
Prepare for war
medium.explanation: The phrase calls for continual lament and prayer day and night.
medium.q: What does “give thyself no rest” mean in this context?

answers: Prayer should be brief and restrained
The grief and prayer should be poured out fully and without holding back
The heart should remain hidden
challenge.explanation: The image of water emphasizes a complete and open expression of grief before the Lord.
challenge.q: What does the comparison “pour out thine heart like water” emphasize?

answers: The lament connects the city’s destruction with the real suffering of individuals
The destruction was only symbolic
The children and slain people are unrelated to the disaster
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from the cry of the city to hunger, death, and the suffering of young and old.
challenge.q: What does the movement from the general cry to the suffering children and slain people show?

answers: Many people successfully fled
No one remained alive or escaped from the calamity being described
The enemies left before the battle
challenge.explanation: The closing verse stresses the completeness and severity of the destruction.
challenge.q: What is the meaning of the conclusion that none escaped or remained?
